eras.name: Before the Nations
eras.power: No empire yet — clans and city-states
eras.captivity: None. Humanity is scattered, not enslaved.
rulers: Nimrod, first to build an empire (Gen 10:8–10)
eras.note: Creation, the Flood, and Babel. Josephus dates the whole stretch from Adam to Isaac at 3,833 years.

eras.name: The Patriarchs
eras.captivity: None — but the 400 years of bondage are foretold to Abram (Gen 15:13).
eras.note: One family walking through other people's kingdoms, owning nothing but a burial cave and a promise.

eras.name: Egypt and the Exodus
eras.captivity: EGYPTIAN BONDAGE. Israel is enslaved for generations under the pharaohs.
eras.note: The first captivity, and the pattern for every one after it: oppression, a cry, a deliverer, a covenant.

eras.name: The Wilderness
eras.power: Israel under Moses; no settled land
eras.captivity: Freed from Egypt, not yet in the land. A generation dies in the desert.
eras.note: Where the Law is given. Nearly every statute in the Bible is written in this forty-year window.

eras.name: The Conquest
eras.captivity: None. Israel is the invading power.
eras.note: Land is taken and divided by lot. The tribal map of the rest of the Old Testament is drawn here.

eras.name: The Judges
eras.power: No central government — 'every man did that which was right in his own eyes'
eras.captivity: SEVEN OPPRESSIONS in cycles: Mesopotamia, Moab, Canaan under Jabin, Midian, Ammon, and Philistia.
eras.note: Not a captivity in a foreign land but repeated subjugation at home. The book keeps count of the years.

eras.name: The United Kingdom
eras.power: Israel at its height; Egypt and Assyria both weak
eras.captivity: None. The nation is free, wealthy, and building.
eras.note: One throne over twelve tribes. The Temple is built. It lasts three reigns.

eras.name: The Divided Kingdom
eras.power: Two rival Hebrew kingdoms; Assyria rising
eras.captivity: None yet, but tribute and vassalage begin.
rulers: ISRAEL (north): Jeroboam I → Ahab → Jehu → Hoshea
eras.note: Ten tribes north under Jeroboam, two tribes south under Rehoboam. Most of the prophets speak into this split.

eras.name: The Assyrian Captivity
eras.captivity: THE TEN TRIBES ARE DEPORTED. Shalmaneser takes Samaria; the north never returns.
eras.note: Judah survives alone for another 130 years and watches what happened to its brother.

eras.name: The Babylonian Captivity
eras.captivity: JUDAH IS DEPORTED IN THREE WAVES (605, 597, 586). Jerusalem and the Temple are burned. Seventy years.
rulers: Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin and Zedekiah in Judah
eras.note: The exile that produced Ezekiel, Daniel and Lamentations — and the one Jeremiah had timed in advance.

eras.name: The Persian Return
eras.captivity: Ended by decree. Jews are free to return but remain a Persian province.
eras.note: Temple rebuilt, walls rebuilt, the Law read aloud in public. The Old Testament closes here.

eras.name: Greek Rule
eras.power: Macedon, then Ptolemaic Egypt and Seleucid Syria
eras.captivity: Occupation and forced Hellenization under Antiochus IV; brief independence under the Maccabees.
eras.note: No canonical book is written here — the four hundred silent years. Josephus is the main witness.

eras.name: Roman Rule
eras.captivity: Client kingdom, then direct rule by prefects. Jerusalem is destroyed again in AD 70.
eras.note: The Gospels, Acts and every letter in the New Testament are written under Roman power.

sections.note: Torah — the five books of Moses

sections.name: Poetry & Wisdom
sections.note: Songs, proverbs and the problem of suffering

sections.note: The long books of warning and promise

sections.name: Minor Prophets

books.name: Genesis
books.full: The First Book of Moses: Called Genesis
books.scribe: Moses, by long tradition — working, most scholars think, from older family records and oral genealogies. The book itself names no author.
books.summary: The book of beginnings: world, humanity, sin, nations, and one family chosen out of them. It ends with that family safe in Egypt and a coffin waiting to be carried home.
prophecies: Gen 3:15 — the seed of the woman shall bruise the serpent's head
Gen 12:1–3 — in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed
Gen 15:13 — thy seed shall be a stranger in a land not theirs four hundred years
Gen 49:10 — the sceptre shall not depart from Judah
laws: The Sabbath pattern (2:2–3)
Bloodshed answerable to God (9:5–6)
Circumcision as covenant sign (17:10–14)
books.captivity: None yet — but foretold in chapter 15.

moves.n: Creation, fall, flood, Babel — the whole world in eleven chapters.
Called out of Ur, given a covenant, tested on a mountain.
A stolen blessing, twenty years in exile, a wrestling match, a new name.
Sold by his brothers into the empire that will one day enslave them all.

chapters.1: Six days of creation and a seventh of rest. The refrain 'and God saw that it was good' runs through it, and humanity is made in God's image, male and female, and given dominion.
chapters.2: The second account, from ground level: a garden, two named trees, a river in four heads, the naming of the animals, and the making of woman from the man's side.
chapters.3: The serpent, the fruit, the hiding, and the three sentences. Verse 15 — the seed of the woman bruising the serpent's head — is read as the first messianic promise in the Bible.
chapters.4: Cain and Abel. Two offerings, one murder, and a mark of protection on the killer. The chapter closes with Cain's line building the first city and inventing metalwork and music.
chapters.5: The genealogy from Adam to Noah, with ages. Enoch walks with God and is not, for God took him — the only break in the drumbeat of 'and he died'.
chapters.6: The sons of God, the giants, and God's grief that he had made man. Noah is told to build an ark to exact specifications and to take his household aboard.
chapters.7: The flood. Forty days of rain, the fountains of the deep broken up, and the waters prevailing on the earth a hundred and fifty days.
chapters.8: The waters recede. A raven, then a dove three times, and an olive leaf. Noah leaves the ark and builds an altar; God promises seedtime and harvest will not cease.
chapters.9: The covenant with all flesh, sealed by the rainbow. Blood is forbidden as food, and the shedding of human blood made answerable. Noah's drunkenness and the curse on Canaan follow.
chapters.10: The table of nations — seventy descendants of Shem, Ham and Japheth, mapped to peoples and territories. Nimrod appears as the first to be mighty on the earth and the founder of Babel and Nineveh.
chapters.11: The tower of Babel. One language, one plan, and a scattering. The chapter then narrows sharply from all nations to one man: Terah takes his son Abram out of Ur toward Canaan.
chapters.12: THE CALL. Get thee out of thy country, and I will make of thee a great nation — in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed. Abram goes, and then goes down to Egypt and lies about his wife.
chapters.13: Abram and Lot separate over grazing rights. Lot chooses the well-watered plain toward Sodom; God restates the promise of the land to Abram, telling him to walk its length and breadth.
chapters.14: A war of four kings against five. Lot is taken captive and Abram rescues him with 318 trained men. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the most high God, brings bread and wine and receives a tithe.
chapters.15: The covenant cut. Abram is told to count the stars, and he believed in the LORD, and he counted it to him for righteousness. He is also told his seed will be strangers in a land not theirs FOUR HUNDRED YEARS.
chapters.16: Sarai gives Hagar to Abram, then despises her when she conceives. Hagar flees, meets the angel of the LORD at a well, and names him Thou God seest me. Ishmael is born.
chapters.17: Circumcision given as the sign of the covenant. Abram becomes Abraham and Sarai becomes Sarah; the promise of a son to a hundred-year-old man is made specific, and Abraham laughs.
chapters.18: Three visitors at Mamre. Sarah laughs behind the tent door and is questioned about it. Then Abraham bargains God down from fifty righteous men to ten over the fate of Sodom.
chapters.19: The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. Lot is dragged out by the angels; his wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. The chapter ends with the incest that produces Moab and Ammon.
chapters.20: Abraham repeats the lie about Sarah, this time to Abimelech of Gerar, who is warned in a dream and confronts him. Abraham's explanation is that she is in fact his half-sister.
chapters.21: Isaac is born and Sarah's laughter changes meaning. Hagar and Ishmael are sent away and rescued at a well, and Abraham makes a treaty with Abimelech at Beersheba.
chapters.22: THE BINDING OF ISAAC. Three days' walk, the wood carried by the son, the question about the lamb, and the ram caught in a thicket. God swears by himself to bless Abraham's seed.
chapters.23: Sarah dies at 127. Abraham negotiates publicly with the sons of Heth and pays four hundred shekels for the cave of Machpelah — the only land he ever owns in the country he was promised.
chapters.24: The longest chapter in Genesis: a servant sent to find Isaac a wife, a prayer at a well answered before he finishes it, Rebekah watering ten camels, and her decision to go.
chapters.25: Abraham dies and is buried by both sons. Then Esau and Jacob wrestle in the womb, and Esau sells his birthright for a bowl of red lentils because he is hungry.
chapters.26: Isaac's chapter — famine, the same lie about his wife, and a series of contested wells. God renews the covenant with him directly at Beersheba.
chapters.27: The stolen blessing. Goatskins on the hands, venison substituted, and a blind father deceived. Esau's cry is that his brother has now taken both birthright and blessing; Jacob runs.
chapters.28: Jacob sleeps with a stone for a pillow at Bethel and sees a ladder set up on the earth reaching to heaven. God repeats the promise to him, and he makes a conditional vow.
chapters.29: Jacob meets Rachel at the well and serves seven years for her, which seemed to him but a few days. Laban substitutes Leah in the dark, and he serves seven more.
chapters.30: The birth contest between two sisters and two handmaids produces eleven sons and a daughter. Then Jacob's speckled-and-spotted breeding scheme turns Laban's flocks into his own.
chapters.31: Jacob flees with his family and herds. Rachel steals her father's household gods and sits on them. Laban catches up; they build a stone heap as a boundary neither will cross.
chapters.32: Jacob wrestles a man until daybreak at Peniel, refuses to let go without a blessing, and is renamed ISRAEL. He limps away, and Esau is coming with four hundred men.
chapters.33: The brothers meet. Esau runs, embraces him, and weeps; the feared reckoning never comes. Jacob sends the gifts anyway and settles at Shechem.
chapters.34: Dinah is violated at Shechem. Simeon and Levi use circumcision as a trap and kill every male in the city while they are recovering — an act Jacob is still condemning on his deathbed.
chapters.35: Back to Bethel: idols buried under an oak, the name Israel confirmed, Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin, and Isaac is buried by both his sons.
chapters.36: The generations of Esau — the dukes and kings of Edom. A whole chapter given to the brother who is not the line, listing kings that reigned before any king reigned in Israel.
chapters.37: Joseph's coat, his two dreams, and his brothers' response. Sold to Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver, and a coat dipped in goat's blood carried back to his father.
chapters.38: The interruption: Judah and Tamar. A widow denied her legal right takes it by disguise, and Judah admits she has been more righteous than he. Their son Pharez appears in David's genealogy.
chapters.39: Joseph in Potiphar's house — trusted with everything, propositioned daily, and jailed on a false charge. The refrain is that the LORD was with him, even in prison.
chapters.40: Two dreams in prison: the butler restored, the baker hanged. Joseph asks to be remembered, and the butler forgets him for two full years.
chapters.41: Pharaoh's two dreams. Joseph is shaved and brought from the dungeon, interprets seven fat and seven lean years, proposes a grain policy, and is made second in Egypt at thirty.
chapters.42: The brothers come to buy corn and bow, fulfilling the dream. Joseph accuses them of spying, keeps Simeon, and returns their money secretly. Guilt surfaces in their conversation.
chapters.43: The second journey with Benjamin. Judah pledges himself as surety. Joseph seats them in birth order, which unnerves them, and gives Benjamin five times the portion.
chapters.44: The silver cup planted in Benjamin's sack. Judah, who once sold Joseph, offers to become a slave in his brother's place — the moment the test is designed to produce.
chapters.45: Joseph makes himself known, weeping so loudly the Egyptians hear. Ye thought evil against me, but God meant it unto good. Wagons are sent to bring the whole family down.
chapters.46: Jacob offers sacrifice at Beersheba and is told not to fear going to Egypt. Seventy souls are listed by name, and Joseph meets his father's chariot at Goshen.
chapters.47: Jacob blesses Pharaoh. The famine deepens and Joseph nationalises Egypt's land and livestock, instituting a fifth to Pharaoh — leaving only the priests' land untouched.
chapters.48: Jacob adopts Joseph's two sons as his own and crosses his hands deliberately, putting the younger Ephraim ahead of Manasseh over Joseph's objection.
chapters.49: Jacob's blessings on the twelve tribes, in poetry. Judah is given the lion and the sceptre, with the line that it shall not depart from him until Shiloh come.
chapters.50: Jacob is embalmed in Egypt and carried to Machpelah. The brothers fear reprisal; Joseph reassures them, makes Israel swear to carry his bones up, and the book ends with a coffin in Egypt.

books.name: Exodus
books.full: The Second Book of Moses: Called Exodus
books.scribe: Moses. Ex 24:4 records that he wrote the words of the LORD, and 17:14 that he wrote in a book by command.
rulers: The pharaoh who knew not Joseph
books.summary: Israel goes from brickyard to covenant nation in one generation. Ten plagues break Egypt's grip, the sea opens, and at Sinai a company of freed slaves is given a law and a tabernacle.
prophecies: Ex 3:12 — ye shall serve God upon this mountain
Ex 12:14 — the Passover kept as a memorial for ever
laws: The Ten Commandments (20:1–17)
The Book of the Covenant — civil law (21–23)
Passover and unleavened bread (12)
Tabernacle, priesthood and Sabbath (25–31)
books.captivity: EGYPTIAN BONDAGE — broken in chapter 12.

moves.n: A new pharaoh, a basket in the river, a burning bush.
Each one strikes an Egyptian god; the last one takes the firstborn.
The sea, the manna, the water from the rock, Jethro's advice.
The Ten Commandments and the Book of the Covenant.
Detailed specifications given on the mountain.
Broken tablets, intercession, a second set.
The glory fills it, and the book stops.

books.name: Leviticus
books.full: The Third Book of Moses: Called Leviticus
books.scribe: Moses. The book is framed as direct dictation — 'and the LORD spake unto Moses, saying' opens most chapters.
rulers: Aaron and his sons as the first priesthood
books.summary: A manual for living next door to a holy God. Sacrifice, priesthood, clean and unclean, festival calendar, and the year of jubilee.
prophecies: Lev 26 — blessings for obedience and a sevenfold chastening, ending in exile among the nations
laws: Five offerings (1–7)
Clean and unclean (11–15)
Day of Atonement (16)
'Love thy neighbour as thyself' (19:18)
Feasts of the LORD (23)
Sabbath year and jubilee (25)
books.power: None — Israel is encamped at Sinai
books.captivity: Free, unsettled.

moves.n: Burnt, meat, peace, sin and trespass — what each is for.
And Nadab and Abihu killed for strange fire.
Food, childbirth, skin disease, discharge.
One day a year, one man, two goats.
Sexual law, neighbour law, priestly conduct.
Feasts, the sabbath year, and the jubilee.
Terms of the covenant, including exile.

books.name: Numbers
books.full: The Fourth Book of Moses: Called Numbers
books.scribe: Moses. Num 33:2 says he wrote down the stages of the journey by command.
books.summary: Two censuses bracket forty years of wandering. A generation refuses the land at Kadesh and is buried in the desert; their children are counted and led to the edge of Jordan.
prophecies: Num 24:17 — there shall come a Star out of Jacob (Balaam's oracle)
laws: Nazarite vow (6)
Priestly blessing (6:24–26)
Cities of refuge (35)
Inheritance for daughters (27, 36)
books.captivity: Free, wandering.

moves.n: The camp organised tribe by tribe around the tabernacle.
Twelve spies, two good reports, forty years of consequence.
A revolt against Moses, Aaron's rod that budded.
Water from the rock, the bronze serpent, Balaam's oracles.
A new generation counted, land assigned, cities of refuge set.

books.name: Deuteronomy
books.full: The Fifth Book of Moses: Called Deuteronomy
books.scribe: Moses, as recorded sermons on the plains of Moab; the account of his death in chapter 34 was added by another hand, traditionally Joshua.
books.summary: Moses preaches the law a second time to the generation that will actually cross. It is a covenant document: history, stipulations, witnesses, blessings and curses.
prophecies: Deut 18:15 — a Prophet like unto me shall the LORD raise up
Deut 28 — curses that name siege, deportation and scattering among all nations
Deut 30:1–5 — and the LORD will gather thee from all the nations
laws: The Shema (6:4–9)
Law of the king (17:14–20)
Test of a true prophet (18:20–22)
Release of debts every seventh year (15)
books.captivity: Free — with exile written into the covenant as a warning.

moves.n: What God has already done — forty years reviewed.
The law restated: the Shema, the king, the prophet, the courts.
Read aloud from two mountains; exile named as the endpoint.
Moses' song, his blessing, and his unmarked grave.

books.name: Joshua
books.scribe: Joshua for most of it (24:26 says he wrote these words in the book of the law); the closing verses about his death by a later scribe.
books.summary: The land is entered, fought for, and divided by lot. Jericho falls, Ai is lost and won, and the tribes receive borders that will define them for a thousand years.
prophecies: Josh 6:26 — a curse on the man who rebuilds Jericho, fulfilled in 1 Kgs 16:34
laws: Cities of refuge assigned (20)
Levitical cities (21)
books.captivity: None — Israel is the invading force.

moves.n: Jordan stopped, twelve stones, circumcision, the manna ceases.
Jericho, Achan's theft, Ai, Gibeon's trick, the long day.
Borders by lot, Levitical cities, cities of refuge.
An altar nearly starts a civil war; Joshua's last charge at Shechem.

books.name: Judges
books.scribe: Traditionally Samuel, compiling older accounts. The refrain 'in those days there was no king in Israel' shows it was written after the monarchy began.
books.summary: Seven cycles of the same story: Israel forgets, is oppressed by a neighbouring power, cries out, is rescued by a judge, and forgets again. Each deliverer is rougher than the last.
books.captivity: SEVEN OPPRESSIONS: Mesopotamia 8 yrs, Moab 18, Jabin of Canaan 20, Midian 7, Ammon 18, Philistia 40.

moves.n: Incomplete conquest, and the cycle explained in advance.
The early judges; Deborah and Barak against Sisera.
Three hundred men with trumpets — then Abimelech's murderous kingship.
A rash vow and a man who never keeps one.
Two horror stories showing what 'no king in Israel' actually meant.

books.name: Ruth
books.scribe: Unknown; traditionally Samuel. Written down after David, since the book ends by tracing his line.
books.written: c. 1000 BC, about events during the judges
books.summary: A famine, a widow, and a foreign woman who refuses to go home. Set in the worst period of the Old Testament, it is a quiet story about loyalty and legal redemption — and it ends with David's grandfather.
prophecies: Ruth 4:17–22 — the genealogy that runs to David, and through him to Christ
laws: Levirate marriage and the kinsman-redeemer (Deut 25:5–10, worked out in Ruth 4)
Gleaning rights for the poor and the stranger (Lev 19:9–10, seen in Ruth 2)
books.captivity: Local oppressions ongoing.

moves.n: Famine, migration, three deaths, and Ruth's refusal to go back.
Ruth ends up in the field of a kinsman by apparent accident.
Naomi's plan; Ruth asks Boaz to act as redeemer.
A sandal changes hands at the gate; a genealogy runs to David.

books.name: 1 Samuel
books.scribe: Samuel for the early chapters; Nathan and Gad are named in 1 Chr 29:29 as recorders of the rest.
rulers: David, anointed but not yet reigning
books.summary: Israel demands a king so as to be like the other nations. They get Saul, who begins well and unravels; and behind him a shepherd from Bethlehem is quietly anointed.
prophecies: 1 Sam 2:35 — I will raise me up a faithful priest
1 Sam 15:28 — the kingdom rent from Saul and given to a better man
laws: The manner of the king — what a monarchy will cost (8:11–18)
books.captivity: Philistine oppression; the ark itself is captured.

moves.n: Hannah's vow, the boy in the temple, the ark captured and returned.
Israel demands a king; Saul is chosen, then rejected twice over.
Anointed in secret, Goliath, Jonathan's friendship, Saul's spear.
David a fugitive; Saul dies on Gilboa with his sons.

books.name: 2 Samuel
books.scribe: Nathan and Gad, the court prophets, per 1 Chr 29:29.
rulers: DAVID (c. 1010–970) — 7 years in Hebron, 33 in Jerusalem
books.summary: David unites the tribes, takes Jerusalem, and receives a covenant of an everlasting throne — then commits adultery and murder, and spends the rest of the book living in the wreckage.
prophecies: 2 Sam 7:12–16 — the Davidic covenant: I will stablish the throne of his kingdom for ever
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Seven years over Judah in Hebron, then all Israel; Jerusalem taken.
The ark brought up, the covenant of an everlasting throne, victories.
Adultery, murder, Nathan's parable, a child dies.
Rape, fratricide, Absalom's coup, David fleeing barefoot.
Famine, giants, David's psalm, and a census that costs 70,000 lives.

books.name: 1 Kings
books.full: The First Book of the Kings
books.scribe: Compiled by an unnamed scribe — Jewish tradition says Jeremiah — from court records: 'the book of the acts of Solomon' and the chronicles of both kingdoms are cited by name.
rulers: Rehoboam and Jeroboam I — the split
books.summary: Solomon builds the Temple and loses his heart to foreign wives. At his death ten tribes walk out, and the book follows two kingdoms downhill until Elijah faces Ahab on Carmel.
prophecies: 1 Kgs 11:11–13 — I will rend the kingdom from thee
1 Kgs 13:2 — a child named Josiah, three centuries before his birth
books.power: Egypt raids under Shishak; Syria pressures the north
books.captivity: None yet — tribute and vassalage begin.

moves.n: Wisdom asked for, the Temple built, the queen of Sheba, then the foreign wives.
Rehoboam's ultimatum, ten tribes gone, two lines of kings begin.
Drought, ravens, Carmel, the still small voice, Naboth's vineyard.

books.name: 2 Kings
books.full: The Second Book of the Kings
books.scribe: Same compiler as 1 Kings; traditionally Jeremiah, writing during or just after the exile.
books.summary: Both kingdoms run out of time. Samaria falls to Assyria in 722 and the ten tribes vanish into Media; Judah lasts to 586, when Jerusalem is burned and the people carried to Babylon.
themes: The word of the LORD coming true
prophecies: 2 Kgs 20:17–18 — Isaiah tells Hezekiah all shall be carried to Babylon, a century early
2 Kgs 22:16–20 — Huldah's prophecy that Josiah will not see the disaster
books.captivity: BOTH. The northern deportation in 722, the southern in 605/597/586.

moves.n: Elijah taken up; a double portion; healings, sieges and floating iron.
Jehu's purge, decline, and Samaria taken by Assyria in 722.
Hezekiah's deliverance, Manasseh's evil, Josiah's reform, Babylon.

books.name: 1 Chronicles
books.full: The First Book of the Chronicles
books.scribe: Ezra, by long tradition — a priest-scribe writing for the returned exiles. Nine chapters of genealogy show a people re-establishing who they are.
books.written: c. 450–430 BC, about events up to 970
rulers: David, retold for a people with no king
books.summary: The same history as Samuel and Kings, retold after the exile for people rebuilding. It skips the northern kingdom entirely and concentrates on David, the ark, and the plans for the Temple.
prophecies: 1 Chr 17:11–14 — the Davidic covenant restated to a nation without a throne
books.captivity: Returned, but a province.

moves.n: Nine chapters tracing Adam to the returning exiles.
Saul's death, the mighty men listed by name.
Uzzah, the tent, and the promise of an everlasting house.
Materials, Levites, singers, gatekeepers — and the handover to Solomon.

books.name: 2 Chronicles
books.full: The Second Book of the Chronicles
books.scribe: Ezra, by tradition. Cites the records of Nathan, Ahijah, Iddo, Shemaiah and Jehu son of Hanani as sources.
rulers: Cyrus, whose decree ends the book
books.summary: Solomon's Temple to its burning, told through Judah's kings and their reforms. It closes mid-sentence with Cyrus telling the exiles to go home and build.
prophecies: 2 Chr 7:14 — if my people shall humble themselves… then will I heal their land
2 Chr 36:21 — the land kept sabbath seventy years, fulfilling Jeremiah
laws: Sabbath years owed and repaid through exile (36:21)
books.captivity: Ends with the decree of release.

moves.n: Wisdom, Temple, dedication, wealth, Sheba.
Rehoboam through Jehoshaphat, with Judah alone in view.
Athaliah's coup, Joash, Uzziah's leprosy, Ahaz's idolatry.
Hezekiah and Josiah's revivals; then Babylon, and Cyrus.

books.name: Ezra
books.scribe: Ezra the priest and scribe. Chapters 7–10 shift into first person — he is writing about himself.
books.summary: Two returns, eighty years apart. The first rebuilds the altar and the Temple against local opposition; the second brings Ezra with the Law and a hard reform of intermarriage.
prophecies: Ezra 1:1 — the decree of Cyrus, expressly to fulfil the word by Jeremiah
laws: Ezra teaches and enforces the law of Moses in the province (7:10, 25–26)
books.captivity: CAPTIVITY ENDED — 539 BC, by decree.

moves.n: Cyrus's decree, Zerubbabel's caravan, altar and foundation, opposition, temple finished.
Eighty years later: a scribe, a commission, and a painful reform.

books.name: Nehemiah
books.scribe: Nehemiah, cupbearer to Artaxerxes — written as a first-person memoir, possibly edited into place by Ezra.
books.summary: A wall goes up in fifty-two days under armed guard. Then the harder work: reading the Law aloud, confessing, and holding a covenant together against debt, mixed marriage and Sabbath trade.
laws: Debt relief and the return of pledged fields (5)
Sabbath trade shut down at the gates (13:15–22)
books.captivity: Free, walled, still taxed by Persia.

moves.n: Nehemiah's prayer, the king's leave, the night ride, fifty-two days of building under threat.
Ezra reads aloud from morning to midday; the people weep, then covenant.
The city repopulated, dedicated — and abuses returning by the last chapter.

books.name: Esther
books.scribe: Unknown — written by someone with detailed knowledge of the Persian court. Mordecai is the traditional candidate.
rulers: Xerxes I, the Ahasuerus of the book (486–465 BC)
books.summary: The Jews who did not go home come within a decree of extermination. God is never named in the book, and the rescue happens entirely through timing, courage and a king's insomnia.
laws: The feast of Purim established as binding on the Jews and their seed (9:27–28)
books.captivity: Diaspora — free to leave, choosing to stay.

moves.n: Vashti refuses, and a search brings Esther to the palace.
Haman's decree, Mordecai's grief, Esther's fast and first banquet.
The king cannot sleep, reads the chronicles, and Haman's day inverts.
A counter-decree, the Jews defend themselves, Purim established.

books.name: Job
books.scribe: Unknown, and possibly the oldest book in the Bible — the setting is patriarchal, with wealth counted in livestock and no mention of Israel, the Law or the Temple.
books.written: Setting c. 2000–1800 BC; written down far later
rulers: No king — Job is a clan head in the land of Uz
books.summary: A blameless man loses everything, and three friends spend thirty chapters explaining why he must deserve it. God finally answers, and never explains — he asks questions instead.
themes: God's answer as presence, not argument
prophecies: Job 19:25 — I know that my redeemer liveth
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Job loses property, children and health in two days.
Three friends in three rounds; Job answers every one.
A younger man who has been listening the whole time.
Out of the whirlwind, in questions — and Job's restoration.

books.name: Psalms
books.scribe: A collection by many hands over ~1,000 years: 73 attributed to David, 12 to Asaph, 11 to the sons of Korah, 2 to Solomon, one to Moses (Ps 90), and about 50 anonymous. Arranged into five books.
rulers: the exiles by the rivers of Babylon
books.summary: Israel's hymnbook and prayer book, covering the whole range from praise to rage. Five books, each closing with a doxology, mirroring the five books of Moses.
prophecies: Ps 2 — thou art my Son
Ps 22 — they pierced my hands and my feet
Ps 110 — a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek
laws: Ps 19 and Ps 119 — extended meditations on the law itself
books.captivity: Ps 137 is written in Babylon.

moves.n: Mostly David. Opens with the two ways and closes with a doxology.
Korah and David; ends with the note that David's prayers are ended.
Asaph's psalms; the darkest section, wrestling with national collapse.
Opens with Moses' psalm; the LORD reigns over the nations.
Songs of degrees, the great acrostic 119, and five closing hallelujahs.

books.name: Proverbs
books.scribe: Solomon chiefly (1:1; 10:1; 25:1), with sections by Agur (30) and King Lemuel (31). Chapters 25–29 were copied out later by Hezekiah's men.
books.summary: Practical wisdom in short lines: money, speech, work, friendship, sex, anger. Wisdom is personified as a woman calling in the street, and the fear of the LORD is where it starts.
laws: Honest weights and measures (11:1; 20:10)
Justice for the poor and the mute (31:8–9)
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Extended speeches urging a son to choose wisdom over the gang and the strange woman.
Hundreds of two-line contrasts on work, speech, money, temper.
Thirty sayings, including a warning against moving a landmark.
Copied out by the king's men two centuries later.
Numerical sayings, and the woman of valour acrostic.

books.name: Ecclesiastes
books.scribe: 'The Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem' — traditionally Solomon in old age.
books.summary: A king with unlimited means tests pleasure, work, wisdom and wealth, and finds each one vapour. The conclusion is not despair but a narrowed life: eat your bread, do your work, fear God.
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Pleasure, building, wealth and wisdom all tested and weighed.
A time to every purpose; the oppression the Preacher keeps seeing.

moves.t: What wisdom can and cannot do
moves.n: Better-than sayings, and the limits of being clever.
Remember thy Creator in the days of thy youth. Fear God and keep his commandments.

books.name: Song of Solomon
books.scribe: Solomon (1:1), who the text says wrote 1,005 songs — this being called the best of them.
books.summary: A love poem between a bride and her beloved, sung back and forth with a chorus of daughters of Jerusalem. Read plainly it is about desire and marriage; read allegorically, about God and his people.
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Longing, praise, and a search through the city at night.
The bridegroom's description of his bride; the garden shut up.
Mutual belonging, and the final claim that love is strong as death.

books.name: Isaiah
books.full: The Book of the Prophet Isaiah
books.scribe: Isaiah son of Amoz, prophet at the royal court in Jerusalem for about sixty years. Jewish tradition holds he was martyred under Manasseh. Some modern scholars divide the book between Isaiah and later disciples writing in his line; the book itself claims one prophet.
rulers: Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser and Sennacherib of Assyria
books.summary: Sixty-six chapters in two halves. Chapters 1–39 confront Judah under Assyrian threat; chapters 40–66 speak past that to exiles in Babylon who had not yet been taken, promising a return, a servant who suffers, and a new heavens and earth.
prophecies: Isa 7:14 — a virgin shall conceive
Isa 9:6 — unto us a child is born… The Prince of Peace
Isa 11:1 — a rod out of the stem of Jesse
Isa 44:28 and 45:1 — CYRUS NAMED as the shepherd who will say to Jerusalem, thou shalt be built
Isa 53 — the suffering servant wounded for our transgressions
Isa 65:17 — new heavens and a new earth
books.captivity: The north falls to Assyria in 722 during Isaiah's ministry. Babylon is named as the next captor a century before it happens.

moves.n: Judah indicted, Isaiah commissioned, Ahaz refuses a sign, a child is promised.
Babylon, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, Tyre — empire by empire.
The earth judged; death swallowed up in victory.
Six woes on those trusting Egypt instead of God; the highway of holiness.
Sennacherib's siege, Hezekiah's illness, and the Babylonian envoys.
Comfort ye my people; Cyrus named; four Servant Songs.
The scope widens to foreigners and eunuchs; new heavens and new earth.

chapters.1: Opening indictment. An ox knows its owner but Israel does not. God says he is sick of sacrifices offered by bloodstained hands — then offers the famous exchange: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.
chapters.2: A vision of the last days: nations streaming to the mountain of the LORD, swords beaten into plowshares. Then the reverse image — the day of the LORD against everything lofty, with men throwing their idols to the moles and bats.
chapters.3: Judah's leadership is stripped away — the judge, the soldier, the elder — and children are left to rule. A long, specific catalogue of the fashions of the women of Zion ends with the finery replaced by a rope and branding.
chapters.4: Short and hinged on hope. Seven women grab one man because the men are dead — but the branch of the LORD is beautiful, and a cloud and fire cover Zion as at Sinai.
chapters.5: The song of the vineyard: God planted it, tended it, and got wild grapes. Six woes follow — on land-grabbers, drunkards, those who call evil good, the self-wise, and corrupt judges.
chapters.6: THE CALL. In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah sees the LORD high and lifted up, the seraphim crying holy, holy, holy. A coal touches his lips, he volunteers, and is told his preaching will harden rather than convert.
chapters.7: Ahaz is under siege from Syria and Israel. Isaiah brings his son Shear-jashub and tells the king to ask for a sign; Ahaz refuses in false piety, and the sign is given anyway — a virgin shall conceive, and shall call his name Immanuel.
chapters.8: The prophet's second son is given the longest name in the Bible, Maher-shalal-hash-baz, as a clock on Assyria's invasion. God is a sanctuary to some and a stone of stumbling to others.
chapters.9: The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light. Unto us a child is born — Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace. The chapter then turns to judgment on the north with a refrain that will not let go.
chapters.10: Assyria is God's axe, and does not know it. The chapter warns the axe against boasting over the one who swings it, and promises that a remnant shall return.
chapters.11: A rod out of the stem of Jesse, with the sevenfold Spirit resting on him — judging not by what his eyes see. Then the peaceable kingdom: wolf with lamb, and a child playing at the asp's hole.
chapters.12: A six-verse song of thanksgiving for the day of return. Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid.
chapters.13: The burden of BABYLON — named as the destroyer more than a century before it destroyed anything. It shall never be inhabited, and wild beasts shall lie there.
chapters.14: The taunt-song over the king of Babylon: how art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning. Oracles against Assyria and Philistia close the chapter.
chapters.15: The burden of Moab. A short, grieving oracle — the prophet says his own heart cries out for Moab, which is unusual in a judgment text.
chapters.16: Moab's oracle continues with an appeal for refuge and a three-year deadline. Isaiah says he will water it with his tears.
chapters.17: The burden of Damascus, which will cease from being a city. Israel is caught in the same sentence — nations rush like waters, and God rebukes them.
chapters.18: The land shadowing with wings, beyond the rivers of Ethiopia. Ambassadors are sent home; God watches from his dwelling place like clear heat, and prunes at the right moment.
chapters.19: The burden of EGYPT — civil war, dried-up Nile, confused counsellors. Then an astonishing turn: an altar to the LORD in the midst of Egypt, and a highway from Egypt to Assyria, with Israel a third with them.
chapters.20: Isaiah walks naked and barefoot for three years as a living sign that Egypt and Ethiopia will be led away stripped. One of the costliest sign-acts in scripture.
chapters.21: The burden of the desert of the sea. A watchman is posted; he reports Babylon is fallen, is fallen — a line Revelation will take up. Also oracles on Dumah and Arabia.
chapters.22: The valley of vision — Jerusalem itself. The city is on the rooftops celebrating while the enemy approaches; they reinforce the walls but do not look to God. Shebna the treasurer is demoted and Eliakim given the key of David.
chapters.23: The burden of TYRE, the merchant city. Its trade will stop for seventy years, then resume — and Isaiah says the merchandise will finally be holiness to the LORD.
chapters.24: The little apocalypse begins. The earth is turned upside down and its inhabitants scattered, priest and people alike; the earth reels like a drunkard under the weight of a broken everlasting covenant.
chapters.25: A song in the middle of the judgment. God spreads a feast of fat things for all people, swallows up death in victory, and wipes away tears from off all faces.
chapters.26: A song sung in the land of Judah. Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee. Also an early resurrection line — thy dead men shall live.
chapters.27: Leviathan is punished; the vineyard of red wine is now kept by God himself night and day. The scattered are gathered by a great trumpet.
chapters.28: Woe to the drunkards of Ephraim. The mocking teachers get precept upon precept, line upon line — and are told a foundation stone is laid in Zion, tried and precious.
chapters.29: Woe to Ariel, the city where David dwelt. The vision has become a sealed book nobody can read; the people draw near with their mouth while their heart is far away.
chapters.30: Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help. Yet the LORD waits to be gracious, and a voice behind them says: this is the way, walk ye in it.
chapters.31: A short reprise of the same warning — the Egyptians are men and not God, their horses flesh and not spirit.
chapters.32: A king shall reign in righteousness, and every man be as a hiding place from the wind. The women at ease are shaken, until the Spirit is poured from on high and the wilderness becomes a field.
chapters.33: Woe to the treacherous spoiler. The question is asked: who among us shall dwell with devouring fire? The answer is a moral one, and the chapter ends with the LORD as judge, lawgiver and king.
chapters.34: Judgment on the nations, with Edom singled out. The imagery is total — the heavens rolled together as a scroll.
chapters.35: The desert shall rejoice and blossom as the rose. Eyes opened, ears unstopped, the lame man leaping — and a highway called the way of holiness, where no lion goes.
chapters.36: HISTORY BEGINS. Sennacherib's field commander stands outside Jerusalem's wall and delivers a propaganda speech in Hebrew so the soldiers on the wall can hear it.
chapters.37: Hezekiah takes the threatening letter into the Temple and spreads it before the LORD. Isaiah answers; the angel of the LORD strikes 185,000 in the Assyrian camp, and Sennacherib goes home and is murdered by his sons.
chapters.38: Hezekiah is told to set his house in order, prays, weeps, and is given fifteen more years — confirmed by the shadow going back ten degrees. His written psalm of recovery is included.
chapters.39: THE HINGE OF THE BOOK. Hezekiah shows Babylonian envoys everything in his treasury, and Isaiah tells him it will all be carried to Babylon, and his sons made eunuchs there. Hezekiah's reply is that at least there will be peace in his own days.
chapters.40: Comfort ye, comfort ye my people. A voice cries in the wilderness; all flesh is grass; the nations are a drop in a bucket. It closes with those who wait upon the LORD mounting up with wings as eagles.
chapters.41: God calls the nations into court to argue their case. Fear thou not, for I am with thee — I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness. Idols are challenged to predict anything at all.
chapters.42: THE FIRST SERVANT SONG. Behold my servant, whom I uphold — a bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench. He is given as a covenant to the people and a light to the Gentiles.
chapters.43: Fear not, for I have redeemed thee; when thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee. God announces he is doing a new thing, and blots out transgressions for his own sake.
chapters.44: An extended satire on idol-making: a man cuts a tree, burns half for warmth, roasts meat over it, and worships the rest. The chapter closes by naming CYRUS as the one who will say to Jerusalem, thou shalt be built.
chapters.45: God addresses Cyrus by name as his anointed, saying he girded him though Cyrus did not know him. I form the light and create darkness. Every knee shall bow — a line Paul will quote twice.
chapters.46: Bel bows and Nebo stoops. The idols must be carried by their worshippers; God says he has carried Israel from the belly and will carry it to old age and grey hairs.
chapters.47: The fall of Babylon addressed as a woman losing her throne. Her astrologers and monthly prognosticators are told to stand up and save her, and cannot.
chapters.48: God says he told them beforehand precisely so they could not credit their idols. O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments — then had thy peace been as a river.
chapters.49: THE SECOND SERVANT SONG. Called from the womb, given as a light to the Gentiles that he may be salvation to the ends of the earth. Zion says God has forgotten her; the answer is a mother forgetting her nursing child.
chapters.50: THE THIRD SERVANT SONG. The servant gives his back to the smiters and his cheeks to those who pluck out the hair. He is not confounded, having set his face like a flint.
chapters.51: Look to the rock whence ye are hewn. Jerusalem is told to wake up, having drunk the cup of trembling to its dregs — and the cup is taken out of her hand.
chapters.52: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings. The last three verses open the fourth Servant Song: his visage was so marred more than any man.
chapters.53: THE SUFFERING SERVANT. Despised and rejected, wounded for our transgressions, bruised for our iniquities. He opened not his mouth. He made his grave with the wicked — and shall see his seed and prolong his days.
chapters.54: Sing, O barren. The tent is enlarged and the stakes strengthened. God calls his anger a small moment and swears by the waters of Noah never to be wroth in that way again.
chapters.55: Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters. My thoughts are not your thoughts — and the word that goes out of God's mouth shall not return void.
chapters.56: The scope widens dramatically: foreigners and eunuchs, previously excluded from the assembly, are promised a name better than sons and daughters. Mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people.
chapters.57: A rebuke of idolatry conducted under every green tree, alongside the line that the righteous perishes and no man lays it to heart. God dwells with the humble and contrite.
chapters.58: The fast God chooses is not bowed heads and sackcloth but loosing the bands of wickedness, feeding the hungry, and housing the poor. Also the promise attached to keeping the sabbath.
chapters.59: Your iniquities have separated between you and your God. A blunt confession of national injustice — and God, seeing no intercessor, puts on righteousness as a breastplate himself.
chapters.60: Arise, shine, for thy light is come. Nations and kings come to the brightness of thy rising; gold and incense are brought, gates stay open day and night, and the sun is no longer needed.
chapters.61: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek — the passage Jesus read at Nazareth, stopping mid-verse. Beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning.
chapters.62: Jerusalem is renamed — no more Forsaken and Desolate, but Hephzibah and Beulah. Watchmen are set on the walls who are told not to keep silent.
chapters.63: The figure treading the winepress alone, garments stained red. Then a long remembrance of God's mercies of old, and a plea: doubtless thou art our father, though Abraham be ignorant of us.
chapters.64: The prayer continues — oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens and come down. We are all as an unclean thing, and our righteousnesses as filthy rags. Yet thou art the potter, and we are the clay.
chapters.65: God answers: I am found of them that sought me not. Judgment on the idolaters, then the creation of new heavens and a new earth, where the infant does not die and men enjoy the work of their hands.
chapters.66: The closing chapter. Heaven is God's throne — where is the house you build me? He looks instead to the poor and contrite. Zion gives birth in a day, the nations are gathered to see his glory, and the book ends on both the new heavens and an unquenched fire.

books.name: Jeremiah
books.full: The Book of the Prophet Jeremiah
books.scribe: Jeremiah of Anathoth, a priest's son, dictating to BARUCH the son of Neriah, who wrote the scroll (36:4) — rewrote it after King Jehoiakim burned it (36:32).
rulers: ZEDEKIAH, the last king of Judah
books.summary: Forty years of warning nobody wanted, delivered while the city was actually falling. Jeremiah is beaten, jailed in a cistern, and finally dragged to Egypt — and told to buy a field as a sign that the land would be lived in again.
prophecies: Jer 25:11–12 — SEVENTY YEARS of Babylonian service, then Babylon punished
Jer 29:10 — after seventy years I will visit you and cause you to return
Jer 31:31–34 — a new covenant written in the heart
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN. Jeremiah lives through all three deportations and the burning of the Temple.

moves.t: The call and the early warnings
moves.n: A prophet from before birth; the almond rod, the potter's wheel, the Temple sermon.
Plots on his life, and Jeremiah's bitter complaints to God.
The line of Judah's last kings, and the letter promising seventy years.
The new covenant, and a field bought while the army is at the gate.
The scroll burned, the cistern, the city taken.
Oracles against nine nations, and an appendix on the fall.

books.name: Lamentations
books.scribe: Jeremiah, by tradition — the KJV title says so outright. Five poems, four of them acrostics running through the Hebrew alphabet.
books.written: c. 586 BC, immediately after the fall
rulers: No king — Zedekiah blinded and deported
books.summary: Five funeral poems for a burned city, written by someone who watched it happen. The centre of the middle poem contains the line about mercies new every morning — placed exactly at the structural heart.
themes: Mercy in the middle of ruin
prophecies: Lam 3:22–23 — his compassions fail not, they are new every morning
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN — written in the smoke.

moves.n: An acrostic lament for a widowed capital.
The unbearable claim that God did this.

moves.t: The man who has seen affliction
moves.n: A triple acrostic — and at its centre, mercies new every morning.
Gold dimmed; the horror of the siege recounted plainly.
Not an acrostic. Turn thou us unto thee, and we shall be turned.

books.name: Ezekiel
books.full: The Book of the Prophet Ezekiel
books.scribe: Ezekiel son of Buzi, a priest deported in the second wave, prophesying by the river Chebar in Babylon. He dates his own visions precisely, to the day.
books.summary: A priest who never got to serve in a temple, given visions of one. Wheels and living creatures, a valley of dry bones, and a measured blueprint for a house that has not been built.
prophecies: Ezek 36:26 — a new heart and a new spirit
Ezek 37 — the dry bones: these bones are the whole house of Israel
Ezek 40–48 — the measured temple and the river from the threshold
laws: Ezek 18 — the soul that sinneth, it shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN — he was taken in the 597 deportation.

moves.n: The wheels, the living creatures, the scroll he is made to eat.
Sign-acts: a brick, shaved hair, a packed bag; the glory leaves the Temple.
Seven nations, with Tyre and Egypt at length.
The watchman, the shepherds, the dry bones, Gog.
Measured to the cubit, with a river rising from the door.

books.name: Daniel
books.scribe: Daniel, taken to Babylon as a youth of the royal seed and trained for the king's service. Chapters 1–6 are told about him; 7–12 are written in the first person.
books.summary: Six chapters of court survival and six of vision, spanning seventy years and three empires. Daniel outlasts the kingdom that captured him and is still in office when Cyrus lets the exiles go.
prophecies: Dan 2 — the image of gold, silver, brass and iron: four kingdoms and a stone cut without hands
Dan 7 — four beasts and one like the Son of man given an everlasting dominion
Dan 8 — the ram and the he-goat, named as Media-Persia and Greece
Dan 9:24–27 — the seventy weeks
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN, from the first deportation of 605 to the Persian release.

moves.n: The diet, the dream, the furnace, the writing on the wall, the lions.
Four beasts, ram and goat, seventy weeks, and a final long revelation.

chapters.1: Nebuchadnezzar's first deportation, 605 BC. Four young captives of royal blood are enrolled in a three-year Babylonian education. Daniel asks for pulse and water instead of the king's meat, and proposes a ten-day trial.
chapters.2: The king demands his wise men tell him the dream as well as its meaning, on pain of death. Daniel describes the image of gold, silver, brass and iron with feet of clay — four kingdoms — and a stone cut without hands that becomes a mountain.
chapters.3: The golden image on the plain of Dura and an orchestra as the signal to bow. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego answer that God is able to deliver them, but if not, they still will not bow. A fourth figure walks in the furnace.
chapters.4: Nebuchadnezzar's own account, written in the first person as a public proclamation. A tree cut down, seven times passing over him, and a king who eats grass like an ox until he lifts his eyes to heaven.
chapters.5: Belshazzar's feast, using the vessels taken from the Temple. A hand writes on the plaster: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN. Daniel reads it as counted, weighed, divided — and Babylon falls that night.
chapters.6: A new empire, and a law that no petition may be made to anyone but the king for thirty days. Daniel opens his windows toward Jerusalem and prays as he did before. The lions' den, and Darius fasting all night.
chapters.7: The visions begin. Four beasts out of the sea — lion, bear, leopard, and a dreadful fourth with ten horns. The Ancient of days sits, and one like the Son of man is given a dominion that shall not pass away.
chapters.8: A ram and a he-goat, and the angel Gabriel names them outright: the ram is Media and Persia, the goat is Greece. The little horn that follows, and the 2,300 days.
chapters.9: Daniel reads Jeremiah and works out that the seventy years are nearly up. His prayer of confession is interrupted by Gabriel with the vision of SEVENTY WEEKS — the most debated timeline in scripture.
chapters.10: A three-week fast by the river Hiddekel, and a vision that leaves him with no strength. A messenger explains he was withstood twenty-one days by the prince of the kingdom of Persia.
chapters.11: The most detailed predictive chapter in the Old Testament — kings of the north and south in sequence, matching the Ptolemies and Seleucids so closely that its dating is a standing argument among scholars.
chapters.12: The close: a time of trouble such as never was, many that sleep in the dust awakening, and Daniel told to shut up the words and seal the book. Go thy way till the end be, for thou shalt rest.

books.name: Hosea
books.scribe: Hosea son of Beeri, prophet to the northern kingdom — the only writing prophet native to the north.
rulers: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah of Judah
books.summary: God tells a prophet to marry a woman who will be unfaithful, and then to take her back, so the nation can see its own marriage from the outside. The last of the northern prophets before 722.
prophecies: Hos 3:4–5 — Israel shall abide many days without a king and without a sacrifice
Hos 11:1 — out of Egypt have I called my son
books.captivity: Writes on the edge of the ASSYRIAN deportation of the north.

moves.n: Gomer, three children with prophetic names, and a purchase back.
Israel's unfaithfulness spelled out — and God's refusal to give up.

books.name: Joel
books.scribe: Joel son of Pethuel. Undated in the text — estimates run from the ninth century to after the exile.
rulers: Uncertain — the book names no king, which is itself a clue
books.summary: A locust plague strips the land bare, and the prophet reads it as a rehearsal for the day of the LORD. Then a promise: the Spirit poured out on all flesh.
prophecies: Joel 2:28–32 — I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, quoted by Peter at Pentecost
laws: Fasting and solemn assembly called (1:14; 2:15)
books.captivity: None named.

moves.n: Four waves strip everything; a call to fast.
An army like locusts — and then the Spirit poured out on all flesh.
The valley of decision; plowshares beaten into swords.

books.name: Amos
books.scribe: Amos of Tekoa, a herdsman and dresser of sycomore fruit — not a professional prophet, and he says so (7:14).
rulers: Amaziah, priest of Bethel, who tries to deport him
books.summary: A southern farmer walks north into a boom economy and tells it that its prosperity is built on crushed people. Eight oracles circle the neighbours before landing on Israel itself.
themes: The day of the LORD as darkness
prophecies: Amos 8:11 — a famine of hearing the words of the LORD
Amos 9:11 — I will raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen
laws: Amos 5:24 — let judgment run down as waters
Condemnation of false balances and selling the poor for shoes (8:5–6)
books.captivity: Predicts deportation beyond Damascus — fulfilled in 722.

moves.n: Six neighbours indicted, then Judah, then Israel itself.
Privilege means accountability; luxury built on the poor.
Locusts, fire, plumbline, summer fruit, the Lord at the altar — and a final restoration.

books.name: Obadiah
books.scribe: Obadiah — nothing else is known of him. The shortest book in the Old Testament, 21 verses.
books.summary: One oracle against Edom, the nation descended from Esau, for standing at the crossroads and cheering while Jerusalem burned. Pride in a rock fortress does not save it.
prophecies: Obad 15 — as thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN — written in its aftermath.

moves.n: Twenty-one verses: pride in the rock, betrayal of a brother, the day of the LORD.

books.name: Jonah
books.scribe: Jonah son of Amittai, named in 2 Kgs 14:25 as a prophet under Jeroboam II. The book is written about him, not by him.
rulers: the king of Nineveh, capital of Assyria
books.summary: A prophet is sent to the capital of the empire that will destroy his country, runs the opposite way, and is furious when the city repents. The book ends on a question God asks him.
prophecies: Jon 1:17 — three days and three nights, cited by Christ as a sign (Mt 12:40)
books.captivity: None yet — Nineveh spared here destroys Israel forty years later.

moves.n: To Joppa, to Tarshish, into the hold, into the sea.
A prayer from the fish's belly, quoting the Psalms.
Eight words of preaching, and a city of 120,000 repents.
A gourd, a worm, a hot wind, and God's closing question.

books.name: Micah
books.scribe: Micah the Morasthite, from a farming town in the Judean lowlands — a contemporary of Isaiah with a very different vantage point.
books.summary: Three cycles of doom and hope, from a country prophet who names the corruption of judges, priests and prophets who take money. He is quoted a century later in Jeremiah's defence trial.
prophecies: Mic 3:12 — Zion shall be plowed as a field
Mic 5:2 — BETHLEHEM EPHRATAH, out of thee shall he come forth
laws: Mic 6:8 — to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God
books.captivity: Names both the Assyrian threat and a Babylonian exile (4:10).

moves.n: Samaria and Jerusalem indicted; land seized by those with power to seize it.
Corrupt leaders — and Bethlehem named as the birthplace of the ruler.
God's lawsuit against his people; what doth the LORD require of thee.

books.name: Nahum
books.scribe: Nahum the Elkoshite. Nothing more is known of him.
books.summary: The sequel to Jonah, 150 years on. Nineveh repented once; now the verdict is final. The city fell in 612 BC, and the book reads like a report filed in advance.
themes: Justice deferred is not justice denied
prophecies: Nah 1:8 and 3:19 — an overrunning flood shall make an utter end of the place
books.power: Assyria at its peak, about to collapse
books.captivity: The north is already gone.

moves.n: Slow to anger, great in power — and a stronghold in trouble.
The attack described as if watched from the wall.
The city that made others childless; there is no healing of thy bruise.

books.name: Habakkuk
books.scribe: Habakkuk — the only prophet whose book is structured as an argument with God rather than a message to people.
books.summary: The prophet asks why God tolerates injustice in Judah, and is told he is raising up the Chaldeans — which is worse. Chapter 3 is his answer: a psalm sung while the fig tree fails.
prophecies: Hab 2:4 — the just shall live by his faith, quoted three times in the New Testament
Hab 1:6 — I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation
books.captivity: Predicts the BABYLONIAN invasion just before it arrives.

moves.n: Why do you tolerate this? — and the answer Habakkuk did not want.
The just shall live by his faith; woes on plunder, greed and idols.
A psalm with musical notation: though the fig tree shall not blossom.

books.name: Zephaniah
books.scribe: Zephaniah, great-great-grandson of Hezekiah — the only prophet with royal blood in his stated genealogy.
rulers: JOSIAH, whose reforms Zephaniah likely helped provoke
books.summary: A sweeping day-of-the-LORD oracle against Judah and the nations, delivered as the young king Josiah begins tearing down the high places. It ends with God singing over his people.
prophecies: Zeph 3:17 — he will joy over thee with singing
books.captivity: None yet — Babylon is one generation away.

moves.n: I will utterly consume all things from off the land.
Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Ethiopia, Assyria — and a call to the meek.
The city rebuked, then a remnant left, and God rejoicing over them with singing.

books.name: Haggai
books.scribe: Haggai, one of the prophets of the return. His four messages are dated to the exact day, all within four months of 520 BC.
books.summary: The exiles came home, laid a foundation, and stopped for sixteen years. Haggai's whole message is: your houses are panelled and God's house lies waste. The work restarted within a month.
themes: The greater glory of the second house
prophecies: Hag 2:9 — the glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former
books.captivity: Returned from BABYLON, rebuilding under Persian licence.

moves.n: Panelled houses, a ruined temple, and a drought nobody connected to it.
The latter glory, a lesson from priestly law, and a signet ring.

books.name: Zechariah
books.scribe: Zechariah son of Berechiah, a priest as well as a prophet, working alongside Haggai.
books.summary: Eight night visions, then oracles reaching far past the rebuilding. More quoted in the passion narratives than any prophet except Isaiah.
prophecies: Zech 4:6 — not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit
Zech 9:9 — thy King cometh… lowly, and riding upon an ass
Zech 11:12–13 — thirty pieces of silver
Zech 12:10 — they shall look upon me whom they have pierced
books.captivity: Returned.

moves.n: Horsemen, horns, a measuring line, Joshua re-robed, a lampstand, a flying roll, chariots.
A delegation asks; the answer is about justice, not calendars.
The king on a donkey, thirty pieces of silver, the pierced one, and the day of the LORD.

books.name: Malachi
books.scribe: Malachi — the name means 'my messenger', and some hold it is a title rather than a personal name. The last voice of the Old Testament.
books.summary: A hundred years after the return, worship has gone cynical: blemished animals on the altar, priests bored, marriages discarded, tithes withheld. Written as six disputes — God states a charge, the people answer back.
prophecies: Mal 3:1 — I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way
Mal 4:5 — I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and dreadful day
laws: Tithes brought into the storehouse (3:8–10)
Divorce condemned (2:14–16)
books.captivity: Free. Then four hundred years of silence before Matthew opens.

moves.n: Blemished sacrifices, contempt for the altar, and faithless divorce.
Robbing God in tithes, the book of remembrance, and Elijah promised.

books.name: 1 Esdras
books.scribe: Unknown — a Greek retelling that draws on Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah, probably compiled by a Jewish writer in Egypt.
books.written: c. 200–150 BC, about events from 622–458 BC
books.summary: The return from exile told again, from Josiah's passover to Ezra's reading of the law. Its one wholly original passage is the contest of the three guardsmen at Darius's court, which Zerubbabel wins by arguing that truth is stronger than wine, kings or women.
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN, ending in the Persian release.

moves.n: The passover, then four kings and the fall of Jerusalem.
Zerubbabel argues that truth is strongest, and wins the return.
Opposition, Darius's decree, and the dedication.
The scribe returns with the law and confronts mixed marriages.

books.name: 2 Esdras
books.scribe: Unknown. A composite: the Jewish apocalypse at its core (chapters 3–14, often called 4 Ezra) was written after the fall of Jerusalem, with Christian material added at both ends.
books.written: core c. AD 90–100, additions 2nd–3rd century AD
rulers: Written under Rome, set in the reign of Artaxerxes
the eagle of the vision, read as Rome
books.summary: Seven visions given to a man who cannot accept what has happened to his city. He argues with the angel Uriel about why God permits the wicked to prosper, and is answered with an eagle, a man from the sea, and a commission to rewrite the burned scriptures.
prophecies: 2 Esd 11–12 — the eagle with twelve wings, interpreted as the empire that will be judged
books.captivity: Written in the shadow of AD 70, voiced as if in Babylon.

moves.n: Later material addressed to a rejected Israel.
Why does God allow this? The angel Uriel answers in riddles.
The mourning woman, the eagle, and the man from the sea.
Ezra dictates ninety-four books over forty days.
Oracles of judgment on the nations.

books.name: Tobit
books.scribe: Unknown. Written partly in the first person as Tobit's own account, then continued in the third person.
rulers: the exiles of Naphtali in Nineveh
books.summary: A domestic story set among the deported northern tribes. A blind father, a desperate young woman, a journey with a stranger who turns out to be the angel Raphael, and a marriage that undoes seven deaths.
laws: Tob 4:15 — do that to no man which thou hatest, an early form of the golden rule
books.captivity: ASSYRIAN — the ten tribes deported to Nineveh and Media.

moves.n: Tobit blinded in Nineveh; Sara accused after seven bridegrooms die.
Tobias sets out with a hired guide and a dog, and catches a fish.
Sara's demon driven off; the money recovered from Gabael.
Sight restored, the guide revealed as Raphael, and Tobit's last words.

books.name: Judith
books.scribe: Unknown. The history is deliberately impossible — Nebuchadnezzar is called king of the Assyrians reigning in Nineveh — which has long been read as a signal that the book is a parable rather than a chronicle.
rulers: 'Nabuchodonosor', king of the Assyrians in the book's own telling
books.summary: A besieged town has agreed to surrender in five days if God does not act. A widow walks into the enemy camp, flatters the general for three nights, and comes back with his head in a bag.
books.power: Assyria as the book names it
books.captivity: Invasion and siege, not deportation.

moves.n: Nabuchodonosor sends Holofernes west; nation after nation submits.
Bethulia's water is cut off and the town agrees to surrender in five days.
A widow rebukes the elders, prays, dresses, and walks out of the gate.
Three nights of flattery, one sword, and a rout.

books.name: Rest of Esther
books.scribe: Unknown — Greek additions inserted into the Hebrew Esther and later gathered at the end, which is why they are traditionally numbered 10–16. They are shown here as chapters 1–7, in the order they appear in the printed Apocrypha.
books.summary: Six passages the Hebrew Esther does not contain: Mordecai's dream and its interpretation, the two royal decrees quoted in full, and long prayers by Mordecai and Esther. Where the Hebrew book never names God, these additions name him constantly.
books.captivity: Diaspora under Persian rule.

moves.n: Two dragons, and a little fountain that becomes a river.
Mordecai reports the eunuchs' conspiracy.
Mordecai and Esther plead before she risks the throne room.

moves.t: The audience and the second decree
moves.n: The king's anger turns; Haman's edict is revoked in full.

books.name: Wisdom of Solomon
books.scribe: Unknown, writing in Solomon's voice — a Greek-speaking Jew of Alexandria, thoroughly trained in Greek philosophy.
rulers: addressed to 'ye that be judges of the earth'
books.summary: An argument that righteousness outlasts death, aimed at Jews tempted to give up on their tradition. It opens with the cynics' speech about life being short so we may as well take what we can, and spends the rest of the book answering it.
prophecies: Wis 2:12–20 — the ungodly plotting against the just man, read by the early church as a passion prophecy
books.captivity: Diaspora — a Jewish minority inside a Greek city.

moves.n: The cynics' speech, and the answer that the souls of the righteous are in God's hand.
Solomon's voice: wisdom preferred before sceptres and thrones.
Adam to the Exodus retold as wisdom's work, with a long analysis of how idolatry began.

books.name: Ecclesiasticus
books.scribe: Jesus son of Sirach of Jerusalem — one of the very few Old Testament-era books whose author names himself. His GRANDSON translated it into Greek in Egypt and wrote the prologue explaining the difficulty of the job.
books.written: written c. 180 BC, translated c. 132 BC
rulers: Simon the high priest, praised in chapter 50
books.summary: The longest book of the Apocrypha and the closest in spirit to Proverbs. A working sage's advice on money, friendship, doctors, table manners, women, slaves and death, closing with a roll call of Israel's famous men.
laws: Sir 38:1 — honour a physician, the earliest Jewish endorsement of medicine as a calling
books.power: Greek rule from Egypt and Syria
books.captivity: Free, but under Hellenistic pressure.

moves.t: The grandson's preface and first counsels
moves.n: On translation, the fear of the Lord, patience and friendship.
Money, speech, women, servants, doctors, dreams, table manners.
Wisdom describes herself as taking root in Jacob.
Old age, children, almsgiving, and a hymn on the works of creation.

moves.t: Let us now praise famous men
moves.n: Enoch to Simon the high priest, in sequence.
A personal thanksgiving and an appeal to the unlearned.

books.name: Baruch
books.scribe: Attributed to Baruch son of Neriah, Jeremiah's scribe. Chapter 6 is a separate work, the Epistle of Jeremy, attached to it.
books.summary: A confession read aloud to the exiles by the river, followed by a poem on wisdom and a promise that Jerusalem will see her children come home. The appended letter is a sustained mockery of idols that cannot save themselves from rust.
themes: Wisdom found only in the law
prophecies: Bar 4:36–37 — look about thee toward the east, and behold thy children gathered from the west
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN — written to and for the deported.

moves.n: Read aloud by the river, admitting the exile is deserved.
Wisdom is found in the book of the commandments; Jerusalem speaks to her children.
Put off the garment of mourning; God will level the mountains for the road home.
A separate letter ridiculing idols that cannot dust themselves.

books.name: Song of the Three Children
books.scribe: Unknown — a Greek addition placed inside Daniel 3, between verses 23 and 24.
books.summary: What the three men said inside the furnace. Azarias prays a confession for the whole nation, then all three sing a long call to every created thing — sun, frost, whales, fowls — to bless the Lord.
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN — set inside the fiery furnace.

moves.n: Azarias's confession, the angel driving out the flame, and the song of all creation.

books.name: Susanna
books.scribe: Unknown — a Greek addition to Daniel, placed before chapter 1 in some manuscripts and after chapter 12 in others.
books.summary: Two respected judges corner a woman in her garden and threaten to ruin her if she refuses them. She refuses, they perjure her to a death sentence, and a young Daniel stops the execution by cross-examining them separately about which tree they saw her under.
laws: The law on false witnesses — Deut 19:18–19 applied to the elders in the closing verses
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN — the exiled community governing itself.

moves.n: Two elders, a false charge, a death sentence, and Daniel's cross-examination.

books.name: Bel and the Dragon
books.scribe: Unknown — a Greek addition to Daniel, told as two detective stories.
books.summary: Daniel proves the idol Bel does not eat its offerings by scattering ashes on the temple floor overnight and showing the king the priests' footprints. He then kills a living dragon with a cake of pitch, fat and hair, and survives a second stay among lions.
books.captivity: Post-exilic, at the Persian court.

moves.t: Bel, the dragon, and the lions
moves.n: Ashes on the floor, a cake of pitch, and a second den.

books.name: Prayer of Manasses
books.scribe: Unknown, written in the voice of King Manasseh of Judah. 2 Chr 33:18–19 refers to a prayer of Manasseh in the records of the kings; this is an attempt to supply it.
rulers: the Assyrian king who took him in chains to Babylon
books.summary: Fifteen verses of penitence from the worst king Judah ever had, written after his captivity broke him. One of the most concentrated confessions in scripture — it never asks for anything but pardon.
books.captivity: Manasseh himself taken with hooks to Babylon (2 Chr 33:11) and later restored.

moves.n: Fifteen verses of confession from a king who had filled Jerusalem with idols.

books.name: 1 Maccabees
books.scribe: Unknown — a Jewish historian writing in Hebrew, sober and closely dated. Widely regarded as the most reliable history in the Apocrypha, and Josephus leans on it heavily.
books.written: c. 100 BC, about events from 175–134 BC
books.summary: The revolt that fills the silence between the Testaments. A Seleucid king outlaws the Jewish religion and puts an idol in the Temple; a village priest refuses to sacrifice, and his five sons fight a guerrilla war that ends in an independent Jewish state.
laws: 1 Macc 2:41 — the ruling that Jews may fight in self-defence on the sabbath, after a thousand died refusing to
books.captivity: OCCUPATION AND FORCED HELLENIZATION — the Temple desecrated in 167 BC, rededicated in 164.

moves.n: Antiochus loots the Temple; Mattathias refuses to sacrifice and starts the revolt.
Victories against long odds, the Temple cleansed, and Judas's death in battle.
Diplomacy with rival Seleucid claimants; treaties with Rome and Sparta.
Tribute lifted, the citadel taken, and a hereditary priest-rulership established.

books.name: 2 Maccabees
books.scribe: An unnamed epitomist, who says outright that he has condensed five books by Jason of Cyrene into one and found the work exhausting.
books.written: c. 124–100 BC, about events from 180–161 BC
rulers: Onias III, the murdered high priest
books.summary: Not a sequel but a parallel account, covering a shorter span with more theology and more horror. It contains the martyrdom of Eleazar and of the mother with seven sons, and the clearest Old Testament-era statement of bodily resurrection.
prophecies: 2 Macc 7:9, 14 — the King of the world shall raise us up unto everlasting life
books.captivity: OCCUPATION — the persecution under Antiochus IV, told from the martyrs' side.

moves.n: Two letters to Egypt, and the epitomist explaining his method.
Heliodorus stopped in the treasury; the high priesthood sold and resold.
Eleazar refuses to fake eating; a mother watches seven sons die.
The revolt gathers, Antiochus dies, the Temple is purified.
Lysias, Nicanor, and the institution of a commemorative day.

books.name: Matthew
books.full: The Gospel According to Saint Matthew
books.scribe: Matthew, also called Levi, a tax collector called from his booth — a man trained to keep records, writing for a Jewish readership.
books.summary: The Gospel that keeps pointing backwards — over sixty quotations from the prophets, and a genealogy that opens the New Testament by tying Jesus to Abraham and David. Built around five great blocks of teaching.
prophecies: Mt 24 — the Olivet discourse: the Temple's destruction, fulfilled in AD 70
laws: The Sermon on the Mount (5–7) — the Law intensified, not repealed
Mt 22:37–40 — the two commandments on which hang all the law and the prophets
books.captivity: Occupation — a client kingdom under Roman prefects.

moves.n: Genealogy, virgin birth, magi, flight to Egypt, baptism, temptation.
The first teaching block: the constitution of the kingdom.
Miracles in series, then the twelve sent out.
Rejection hardens; teaching shifts into parables.
Peter's confession, the transfiguration, and instructions on community.
The triumphal entry, seven woes, and the Olivet discourse.
Arrest, trial, crucifixion, resurrection, go ye therefore.

books.name: Mark
books.full: The Gospel According to Saint Mark
books.scribe: John Mark, companion of Peter and of Paul. Early tradition (Papias, c. AD 130) says he wrote down Peter's preaching — which explains the eyewitness detail and the unflattering portrait of Peter.
rulers: possibly Nero at the time of writing
books.summary: The shortest and fastest Gospel — 'straightway' appears more than forty times. Written for Romans: Aramaic phrases are translated, Jewish customs explained, and the action starts with no genealogy at all.
prophecies: Mk 13 — not one stone shall be left upon another
books.captivity: Occupation.

moves.n: Straightway — healings, storms, feedings, and growing crowds.
Peter's confession, three passion predictions, the road to Jerusalem.
The entry, the cleansed temple, the withered fig tree, the last days.
Gethsemane, trial, crucifixion — and an ending that stops abruptly.

books.name: Luke
books.full: The Gospel According to Saint Luke
books.scribe: Luke, a physician and Paul's travelling companion — the only Gentile author in the Bible. He opens by saying he investigated everything from the first and interviewed eyewitnesses.
rulers: Caesar Augustus, whose census opens the book
books.summary: The most historically anchored Gospel, dating events by emperors and governors. It gives the most attention to women, the poor, Samaritans and outsiders, and holds the parables of the good Samaritan and the prodigal son.
prophecies: Lk 21:24 — Jerusalem trodden down of the Gentiles
books.captivity: Occupation.

moves.n: John and Jesus, with four songs; dated by emperor and governor.
Baptism, genealogy back to Adam, the Nazareth sermon, the twelve.
Ten chapters on the road: the good Samaritan, the prodigal son, Zacchaeus.
The entry, the temple, the widow's mites, the coming judgment.
The supper, the trial, the cross, and a seven-mile walk with a stranger.

books.name: John
books.full: The Gospel According to Saint John
books.scribe: John the apostle, son of Zebedee — who refers to himself only as the disciple whom Jesus loved. Written last, decades after the others.
rulers: Domitian at the time of writing
Pilate and Caiaphas in the narrative
books.summary: Ninety per cent of its material is found in no other Gospel. Built around seven signs and seven 'I am' sayings, and it states its purpose outright in 20:31 — these are written that ye might believe.
prophecies: Jn 14:16 — another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever
laws: Jn 13:34 — a new commandment: that ye love one another
books.captivity: Occupation; the Temple already destroyed by the time of writing.

moves.n: In the beginning was the Word — the Gospel's thesis in eighteen verses.
Seven signs from Cana to Lazarus, each followed by argument.
The basin and towel, the vine, the Comforter, and the high priestly prayer.
Trial before Pilate, the cross, the garden, Thomas, and breakfast on the shore.

books.name: Acts
books.scribe: Luke, writing volume two to the same man, Theophilus. From chapter 16 the narrative shifts to 'we' — the author has joined the journey.
books.summary: Thirty years in which a movement of a hundred and twenty people in one room reaches the capital of the empire. Structured by Jesus's own line in 1:8 — Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, the uttermost part of the earth.
prophecies: Acts 1:8 — the programme statement, fulfilled by the last chapter
Acts 2:16–21 — Peter reads Pentecost as Joel's prophecy fulfilled
laws: Acts 15 — the Jerusalem council rules that Gentile believers are not bound to the Mosaic law
books.captivity: Paul ends the book under house arrest in Rome, preaching without hindrance.

moves.n: Ascension, Pentecost, the first church, Stephen's death.
Philip, Saul's conversion, Cornelius, Antioch, Peter's escape.
Cyprus and Galatia with Barnabas.
The question of Gentile circumcision settled at Jerusalem.
Philippi, Athens, Corinth, Ephesus — and the 'we' passages begin.
Riot, five trials, appeal to Caesar, shipwreck, and two years in a hired house.

books.name: Romans
books.full: The Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Romans
