books.scribe: Paul, dictated to TERTIUS, who inserts his own greeting in 16:22 — one of the few named scribes in scripture.
books.summary: Paul's most systematic letter, written to a church he had not yet visited, laying out sin, justification by faith, the Spirit, the place of Israel, and what all of it means on a Tuesday.
prophecies: Rom 11:25–26 — blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles
laws: Rom 13:1–7 — the believer's obligation to civil authority
Rom 13:10 — love is the fulfilling of the law
books.captivity: None — written in freedom, before the imprisonments.

moves.n: All have sinned — Gentile, Jew and moralist alike.
Abraham as the test case; peace with God.
Dead to sin, free from law, alive in the Spirit — and nothing can separate.
Election, the olive tree, and a hardening that is not permanent.
Living sacrifice, government, the weak brother, and a long list of names.

books.name: 1 Corinthians
books.full: The First Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Corinthians
books.scribe: Paul, with Sosthenes named as co-sender.
books.summary: A troubleshooting letter to a gifted, divided, morally chaotic church in a port city. Factions, a lawsuit, a sex scandal, disorderly worship, and confusion over resurrection — answered one at a time.
prophecies: 1 Cor 15:51–52 — we shall all be changed, at the last trump
laws: Guidance on marriage and singleness (7)
Order in worship and at the Lord's table (11–14)
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Factions answered with the foolishness of the cross.
A scandal, lawsuits between believers, and questions about singleness.
Rights surrendered for the sake of a weaker conscience.
Head coverings, the Lord's supper, spiritual gifts — and chapter 13 in the middle.
The fullest argument in scripture, then the collection and greetings.

books.name: 2 Corinthians
books.full: The Second Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Corinthians
books.scribe: Paul, with Timothy as co-sender — his most personal and least guarded letter.
books.summary: Paul defends his ministry against rivals who called him unimpressive in person. He answers by listing not his successes but his beatings, shipwrecks and sleepless nights.
themes: Weakness as the place of power
laws: Principles of giving — willingly, proportionally, cheerfully (8–9)
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Comfort in affliction, the treasure in earthen vessels, the ministry of reconciliation.
Two chapters on giving for the poor in Jerusalem.
Paul's credentials: beatings, shipwrecks, a thorn, and grace sufficient.

books.name: Galatians
books.full: The Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Galatians
books.scribe: Paul — who notes in 6:11 that he has taken the pen from the scribe to write the ending in his own large hand.
books.summary: The angriest letter in the New Testament, and the only one with no thanksgiving. Teachers had arrived telling Gentile converts they must be circumcised; Paul treats this as a different gospel altogether.
laws: Gal 5:14 — all the law is fulfilled in one word: love thy neighbour as thyself
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Called by no man; a confrontation with Peter at Antioch.
Abraham believed God — the law came 430 years later.
Stand fast in liberty; the works of the flesh and the fruit of the Spirit.

books.name: Ephesians
books.full: The Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Ephesians
books.scribe: Paul, a prisoner — likely a circular letter, since the words 'at Ephesus' are missing from the earliest manuscripts.
books.summary: Three chapters on what is true, three on how to live in it. Written by a man in chains about a church described as seated in heavenly places.
laws: Household order — husbands, wives, children, servants (5:22–6:9)
books.captivity: Paul is himself in Roman custody.

moves.n: Chosen, redeemed, sealed; two walls made one; the mystery revealed.
Unity, new self, household order, and the whole armour of God.

books.name: Philippians
books.full: The Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Philippians
books.scribe: Paul and Timothy, to the first church he planted in Europe.
books.summary: A thank-you letter for a financial gift that turns into a meditation on joy, written from a cell. It contains the hymn of Christ emptying himself.
books.captivity: Written in chains, with greetings from Caesar's household.

moves.n: Thanksgiving from prison; to me to live is Christ.
He made himself of no reputation — and God hath highly exalted him.
Paul's résumé counted as dung; pressing toward the mark.
Rejoice always; I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.

books.name: Colossians
books.full: The Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Colossians
books.scribe: Paul and Timothy, carried by Tychicus alongside the letter to Philemon.
books.summary: Written against a mix of philosophy, angel-worship and dietary rules creeping into the church. Paul's answer is a single tall claim about who Christ is, in 1:15–20.
books.captivity: Paul imprisoned.

moves.n: The image of the invisible God, by whom all things consist.
Philosophy, angel-worship and food rules answered.
Put off, put on; household instructions; greetings including Onesimus.

books.name: 1 Thessalonians
books.full: The First Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Thessalonians
books.scribe: Paul, Silvanus and Timothy — possibly the earliest surviving Christian document.
books.summary: Paul had been run out of Thessalonica after a few weeks and worried about what he left behind. Timothy came back with good news, and this letter is the relief — plus an answer about believers who had died.
prophecies: 1 Thess 4:16–17 — the dead in Christ shall rise first
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Paul recalls the founding visit and Timothy's good report.
Sexual purity, quiet work, and the question of believers who have died.

books.name: 2 Thessalonians
books.full: The Second Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Thessalonians
books.scribe: Paul, Silvanus and Timothy. Paul signs it himself in 3:17 as a mark of authenticity, because a forged letter was circulating.
books.summary: A follow-up correcting a rumour that the day of the LORD had already come. Some had stopped working; Paul tells them to get back to it.
prophecies: 2 Thess 2:3–4 — a falling away first, and the man of sin revealed
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Persecution, and rest promised when the Lord is revealed.
The day has not come; the man of sin must be revealed first.
If any would not work, neither should he eat.

books.name: 1 Timothy
books.full: The First Epistle of Paul the Apostle to Timothy
books.scribe: Paul to Timothy, his younger colleague left in charge at Ephesus.
books.summary: A working manual for running a church: who may lead, how widows are supported, how money corrodes, how to handle accusations against elders.
laws: Qualifications for bishops and deacons (3)
Care of widows and honour of elders (5)
books.captivity: Paul apparently free between imprisonments.

moves.n: False teachers, prayer, and the qualifications for overseers and deacons.
Let no man despise thy youth; widows, elders, slaves, and the love of money.

books.name: 2 Timothy
books.full: The Second Epistle of Paul the Apostle to Timothy
books.scribe: Paul — his last known letter, written from a cold cell asking for a cloak and his books.
books.written: c. AD 66–67, shortly before his death
books.summary: A dying man's charge to his successor. Everyone has left; he asks Timothy to come before winter, and to preach the word in season and out.
prophecies: 2 Tim 3:1–5 — in the last days perilous times shall come
books.captivity: Paul in chains, expecting execution.

moves.n: Stir up the gift; be a good soldier, athlete and farmer.
Perilous times; all scripture is given by inspiration; I have finished my course.

books.name: Titus
books.full: The Epistle of Paul the Apostle to Titus
books.scribe: Paul to Titus, left on Crete to organise the churches there.
books.summary: Short and practical: appoint elders in every city, silence the profiteers, and let every group in the congregation know what a credible life looks like.
laws: Qualifications for elders in every city (1:5–9)
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city.
What each group in the church should be taught.
Obedience to authority, avoiding foolish disputes, and the kindness of God.

books.name: Philemon
books.full: The Epistle of Paul the Apostle to Philemon
books.scribe: Paul, writing personally and offering to cover the debt himself — a single chapter, 25 verses.
books.summary: A private letter about a runaway slave named Onesimus, whom Paul is sending back to his owner — asking that he be received not as a servant but as a brother.
books.captivity: Paul imprisoned; Onesimus legally a fugitive.

moves.n: Twenty-five verses asking a slave-owner to receive a runaway as a brother.

books.name: Hebrews
books.full: The Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Hebrews
books.scribe: Unknown — the one New Testament book whose author is genuinely unidentified. Suggestions since the second century have included Paul, Barnabas, Apollos and Priscilla. The KJV title assigns it to Paul; the text does not.
books.written: c. AD 65–69, before the Temple fell
books.summary: Written to Jewish believers under pressure to go back to the Temple system. Its argument is comparative: better than angels, than Moses, than Aaron, than the old covenant.
laws: Heb 8–10 — the argument that the Mosaic sacrificial law was a shadow now fulfilled
books.captivity: Occupation; the Temple's destruction is imminent.

moves.n: Who the Son is, and why the message must be heeded.
Melchizedek — a priest without genealogy or end.
The old was a shadow; one sacrifice, once, for ever.
The roll call: by faith Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham…
Run with patience; the unshakeable kingdom; final exhortations.

books.name: James
books.scribe: James, brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem church — not the apostle. Josephus records his death by stoning in AD 62.
books.written: c. AD 45–49 — possibly the earliest New Testament letter
books.summary: Practical to the point of bluntness, and closer to Proverbs than to Paul. Faith without works is dead; the tongue is a fire; do not flatter the rich man who walks into your assembly.
laws: Jas 2:8 — the royal law: thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself
books.captivity: Written to the twelve tribes scattered abroad.

moves.n: Count it all joy; be doers of the word, not hearers only.
Do not flatter the rich man; faith without works is dead.
A small member that boasts great things; a fire.
Wars come from within; a warning to the rich; the prayer of faith.

books.name: 1 Peter
books.full: The First Epistle General of Peter
books.scribe: Peter the apostle, written with the help of SILVANUS (5:12), who evidently smoothed the Greek.
books.written: c. AD 62–64, from 'Babylon' — widely read as Rome
books.summary: Written to scattered believers in northern Asia Minor as persecution began to bite. Its counsel is not escape but conduct: live so well that the accusation looks absurd.
books.captivity: Believers described as strangers and pilgrims scattered abroad.

moves.n: Born again to a living hope; a chosen generation, strangers and pilgrims.
Answer with meekness; arm yourselves with the same mind.
Feed the flock; cast all your care upon him.

books.name: 2 Peter
books.full: The Second General Epistle of Peter
books.scribe: Peter, written knowing he had little time left (1:14).
books.summary: A warning about teachers who will monetise the faith, and about scoffers who ask why nothing has happened yet. Peter's answer: one day is with the Lord as a thousand years.
themes: The certainty of the day of the LORD
prophecies: 2 Pet 3:10 — the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night
books.captivity: Occupation.

moves.n: Add to your faith virtue; the prophetic word made more sure.
Merchandise made of you; examples from Noah, Sodom and Balaam.
Scoffers ask where the promise is; one day is as a thousand years.

books.name: 1 John
books.full: The First Epistle General of John
books.scribe: John the apostle, writing late in life to churches he knew well — the tone is that of an old man addressing 'my little children'.
books.summary: Written against an early teaching that Christ had not truly come in the flesh. It gives tests by which anyone can check themselves: do you obey, do you love, do you believe.
books.captivity: Occupation.

moves.n: If we walk in the light; whoever says he abides in him ought to walk as he walked.
Behold what manner of love; try the spirits; God is love.
These things have I written that ye may know that ye have eternal life.

books.name: 2 John
books.full: The Second Epistle General of John
books.scribe: 'The elder' — John, writing to 'the elect lady and her children', either a woman or a congregation. Thirteen verses.
books.summary: A short note on hospitality with a hard edge: love one another, and do not host travelling teachers who deny that Christ came in the flesh.
books.captivity: Occupation.

moves.n: Thirteen verses: love one another, and do not receive those who deny Christ came in flesh.

books.name: 3 John
books.full: The Third Epistle General of John
books.scribe: 'The elder' — John, writing to a man named Gaius. Fourteen verses, the shortest book in the Bible.
books.summary: A letter about three men: Gaius, who houses travelling preachers; Diotrephes, who loves being first and throws them out; and Demetrius, who has a good report of all.
books.captivity: Occupation.

moves.n: Gaius who hosts, Diotrephes who refuses, Demetrius who has a good report.

books.name: Jude
books.scribe: Jude, brother of James — and therefore also a brother of Jesus, though he introduces himself only as a servant.
books.summary: Jude says he meant to write about salvation and had to write about intruders instead. He reaches for examples from Israel, from angels, from Sodom, and quotes Enoch.
prophecies: Jude 14–15 — the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints
books.captivity: Occupation.

moves.n: Twenty-five verses: intruders, historical warnings, Enoch's prophecy, and a doxology.

books.name: Revelation
books.full: The Revelation of Saint John the Divine
books.scribe: John, exiled on Patmos, writing what he was told to write — the only New Testament book that opens by pronouncing a blessing on whoever reads it aloud.
rulers: Domitian, who demanded to be addressed as lord and god
the seven churches of Asia under pressure
books.summary: Letters to seven real churches, then a sequence of visions in sevens — seals, trumpets, bowls — running to a final judgment and a city coming down out of heaven.
prophecies: Rev 1:7 — behold, he cometh with clouds
Rev 20 — the thousand years and the final judgment
Rev 21:1–4 — a new heaven and a new earth, and no more death
books.captivity: John himself banished to Patmos for the word of God.

moves.n: John on Patmos; the one like unto the Son of man among the lampstands.
To seven real churches in Asia, each with a commendation, a charge and a promise.
The throne room, the sealed book, and the Lamb who is worthy to open it.
Judgments in sevens, with interludes of sealing and witness.
The woman, the dragon, two beasts, and the number of his name.
The last plagues, and the fall of the great city.
The rider on the white horse, the thousand years, the great white throne.
A new heaven and a new earth; no temple, no night, no more death.

facts.title: Josephus dates the whole of Genesis at 3,833 years
facts.text: His first book is headed as covering the interval from the Creation to the death of Isaac — three thousand eight hundred and thirty-three years. Every later book carries a similar heading, which makes the Antiquities usable as a running timeline of the Old Testament.

facts.title: Adam's descendants left their discoveries on two pillars
facts.text: Josephus says Seth's line invented the study of the heavenly bodies, and that because Adam had predicted the world would be destroyed once by fire and once by water, they inscribed what they knew on two pillars — one of brick, one of stone — so that whichever survived would carry the knowledge forward. He adds that the stone one remained in his day.

facts.title: Outside historians recorded the ark, and pieces of it were being sold
facts.text: Josephus quotes Berosus the Chaldean, who wrote that part of the ship still existed in Armenia at the mountain of the Cordyaeans, and that people carried off bits of its bitumen to use as amulets against misfortune. He names several other non-Hebrew historians who mention the flood.

facts.title: The Armenians called the landing site 'the Place of Descent'
facts.text: Josephus records the local name given to the spot where the ark grounded, and says its remains were shown to visitors there in his own time.

facts.title: Nimrod's tower was built to be flood-proof, on purpose
facts.text: In Josephus's account Nimrod turned people away from God deliberately, and the tower was raised as insurance — built high enough that the water could not reach it, in revenge for the drowning of their ancestors.

facts.title: Abraham taught the Egyptians arithmetic and astronomy
facts.text: Josephus says that when Abram went down to Egypt he debated with their priests, and that the Egyptians had been ignorant of these sciences until they passed from the Chaldeans to Abram and from Abram to them.

facts.title: Josephus says he saw the pillar of salt himself
facts.text: Writing of Lot's wife turning back to look at Sodom, he adds plainly: for I have seen it, and it remains at this day. Whiston's footnote notes that Clement of Rome, a contemporary, said the same.

facts.title: Moses led an Egyptian army into Ethiopia before he ever led Israel
facts.text: Josephus preserves an episode found nowhere in scripture: Moses was made general of Egypt's forces against an Ethiopian invasion, and won. Tharbis, the daughter of the Ethiopian king, watched him fight from the walls, fell in love with him, and offered to surrender the city if he would marry her.

facts.title: The story of the baby in the river begins with a sacred scribe's prediction
facts.text: Josephus writes that one of the Egyptian scribes warned Pharaoh a child was about to be born among the Israelites who would humble Egypt — which is why the order to drown the boys was given.

facts.title: Josephus describes the manna as still falling in his own day
facts.text: He records that the miraculous food which sustained Israel in the desert continued to appear in that region, and says the whole country was still watered with it when he wrote.

facts.title: The high priest's breastplate stopped shining two centuries before Josephus wrote
facts.text: He says the twelve stones gave off a great brightness before the army marched, which is why Greeks who respected Jewish law called the breastplate the Oracle — and then adds that it left off shining two hundred years before he composed his book, God being displeased at the transgression of his laws.

facts.title: Josephus reads the tabernacle as a model of the universe
facts.text: He interprets its three divisions, the seven lamps and the high priest's garments as representing the cosmos — an approach he takes from Philo. Whiston's footnote pushes back, arguing that Jewish emblems should be read by Jewish rather than Greek ideas.

facts.title: Josephus gives Balaam a whole chapter and calls him a prophet
facts.text: Rather than treating him only as a villain, Josephus devotes a chapter to what kind of man Balaam actually was, and reports the oracles he was unable to withhold even when paid to curse.

facts.title: Og's iron bed was still shown as evidence
facts.text: Josephus says people could judge the giant's size from the bed taken at Rabbath, the royal city of the Ammonites — iron, four cubits wide and more than nine long.

facts.title: Josephus preserves a captured king's confession
facts.text: Adonibezek, taken with his fingers and toes cut off, is quoted as saying he had done exactly the same to seventy-two kings, and now found he had not escaped God's notice.

facts.title: The place called Jaw-bone got its name from Samson
facts.text: Josephus notes that the site had no particular name before, and was called the Jaw-bone afterwards because of what Samson did there. He then adds that Samson boasted the victory was his own courage rather than God's help.

facts.title: Josephus gives Goliath's armour in detail
facts.text: He describes the giant of Gath and the encounter with the shepherd at length, including the weight of the armour and the reaction of both armies.

facts.title: David reigned seventy years old, forty years a king
facts.text: Josephus closes David's life with a précis: seven years and six months in Hebron over Judah, thirty-three in Jerusalem over the whole country, and a character assessment calling him a man of valour beyond the ordinary.

facts.title: Solomon and Hiram of Tyre had a riddle contest with money on it
facts.text: Josephus quotes the Tyrian historians Dius and Menander: Solomon sent riddles to Hiram, with a penalty for whoever could not solve them. Hiram paid heavily at first, then found a man of Tyre named Abdemon who could solve them, and won the money back.

facts.title: Josephus says the Tyrian public records could still be consulted
facts.text: He points readers to the archives of Tyre as independent confirmation of the correspondence between Solomon and Hiram over timber for the Temple — an unusual appeal to a foreign document to verify a biblical account.

facts.title: Shalmaneser moved the ten tribes into Media and imported the Cutheans
facts.text: Josephus's chapter heading states it flatly: Samaria taken by force, the ten tribes transplanted into Media, and the nation of the Cutheans brought into their country in their place. These settlers are the origin of the people later called Samaritans.

facts.title: Josephus cites Herodotus and Berosus on Sennacherib's disaster
facts.text: He recounts the destruction of the Assyrian army outside Jerusalem and then reaches for external historians, noting where their accounts touch his own — and records that Sennacherib was murdered by his own sons after returning home.

facts.title: Hezekiah's fifteen extra years came with a sign of the shadow
facts.text: Josephus retells the king's illness, his prayer, and Isaiah's message that he would recover within three days and live fifteen years more — noting that Hezekiah found it hard to believe given how sore the disease was.

facts.title: Cyrus released the Jews because he read Isaiah's prophecy about himself
facts.text: Josephus says Cyrus was shown the book Isaiah left behind, in which God had said his will was that Cyrus should send the people back and build the temple. Reading his own name, Cyrus was seized with ambition to fulfil what was written — and issued the decree.

facts.title: Josephus dates the Cyrus prophecy to 140 years before the Temple fell
facts.text: He states the interval outright, which places Isaiah's naming of Cyrus long before either the Babylonian destruction or the Persian rise — and he treats the gap as the point of the story.

facts.title: Isaiah was the king's reference for future events
facts.text: Writing of Hezekiah, Josephus says the king was untroubled by Assyrian threats because he relied on his own piety and on Isaiah the prophet, by whom he inquired and accurately knew all things to come.

facts.title: The seventy years were counted, and Josephus counts them
facts.text: Opening his account of Cyrus, he specifies that the first year of that reign was the seventieth from the day the people were removed out of their own land into Babylon — exactly as foretold by Jeremiah before the city was destroyed.

facts.title: Josephus says Jeremiah's lament for Josiah was still extant
facts.text: He reports that the prophet composed an elegy for the dead king which remained in existence in his own day — a work distinct from the book of Lamentations.

facts.title: Josephus notes that two prophets contradicted each other about Zedekiah
facts.text: Jeremiah said the king would be taken to Babylon; Ezekiel said he would not see it. Zedekiah concluded both were lying and believed neither — and both turned out true, since he was blinded before being carried there.

facts.title: He records that Ezekiel wrote two books
facts.text: Josephus mentions Ezekiel leaving two books behind concerning these events — a detail that has been argued over ever since, since only one survives.

facts.title: Daniel built a tower at Ecbatana that was still standing
facts.text: Josephus describes it as a most elegant building, wonderfully made, preserved to his own day, and looking to anyone who saw it as though it had been finished that very morning. He says the Median and Persian kings were buried there.

facts.title: Josephus refuses to explain the stone in Nebuchadnezzar's dream
facts.text: He relays the whole image of gold, silver, brass and iron — then stops. He says he has undertaken to describe things past and present, not things future, and tells the curious reader to go and read the book of Daniel for themselves.

facts.title: Alexander the Great was shown the book of Daniel in Jerusalem
facts.text: Josephus writes that when Alexander entered the city, the high priest showed him the passage declaring that one of the Greeks would destroy the empire of the Persians. Alexander concluded he was the person meant, and granted the Jews their own laws and exemption from tribute in the seventh year.

facts.title: Josephus rates Daniel above the other prophets, and says why
facts.text: His reasoning is that Daniel did not only foretell things to come, as the others did, but fixed the time at which they would happen — which is what he thinks makes the book difficult for its critics.

facts.title: Cyrus sent back the Temple vessels by a named treasurer
facts.text: Josephus records the return of the vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken, committed to Mithridates the treasurer, and reproduces the text of Cyrus's letter to the governors in Syria ordering material support for the rebuilding.

facts.title: The decree was found years later, filed in a tower in Media
facts.text: When the rebuilding was challenged under Darius, a search of the royal records turned up Cyrus's original order at Ecbatana — the same tower Josephus attributes to Daniel.

facts.title: Josephus tells the Samaritan half of the wall-building story
facts.text: He gives an extended account of Sanballat, and of the rival temple built on Mount Gerizzim after the high priest's brother married Sanballat's daughter and was expelled from Jerusalem — the origin of the division John 4 assumes.

facts.title: Josephus retells Esther with the Persian court documents included
facts.text: His version of the reign of Artaxerxes reproduces the decrees at length, and treats the deliverance as the founding of a festival still kept by the Jews in his own time.

facts.title: Josephus knew Jonah as a court prophet, not just a man in a fish
facts.text: He recounts Jonah's mission to Nineveh alongside his role under Jeroboam, treating him as part of the political history of the northern kingdom rather than an isolated story.

facts.title: Nineveh fell about as Nahum said it would
facts.text: Josephus quotes Nahum's oracle against the city at length and then reports the fall of the Assyrian capital, treating the prophecy as a dated prediction with a checkable outcome.

facts.title: The four hundred silent years are not silent in Josephus
facts.text: Between Malachi and Matthew the Bible says nothing. Josephus fills the gap across Books XI to XVII: Alexander, the Ptolemies, Antiochus IV, the Maccabean revolt, the Hasmonean priest-kings, Pompey's entry into the Temple, and the rise of Herod.

facts.title: The Septuagint was made by seventy-two translators under Ptolemy
facts.text: Josephus gives a full account of how the Hebrew law came to be translated into Greek for the library at Alexandria — the version most New Testament quotations of the Old Testament follow.

facts.title: The three sects were already in place before the Gospels open
facts.text: Josephus describes the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes as established parties with distinct positions on fate, the soul and the resurrection — which is the background to nearly every argument Jesus has with them.

facts.title: Herod put a golden eagle over the Temple gate, and it cost lives
facts.text: Josephus reports that young men pulled the Roman emblem down and were executed for it, and records Herod's own speech pointing out how much the Temple had cost him — more than the Hasmoneans had managed in a hundred and twenty-five years.

facts.title: Herod's Temple is the building the disciples were admiring
facts.text: Josephus devotes a long passage to the rebuilding, describing the scale of the platform and the stonework. When the disciples point out the great stones in Matthew 24, this is the structure they mean — and it was destroyed within a lifetime.

facts.title: Josephus describes John the Baptist independently of the Gospels
facts.text: He calls John a good man who commanded the Jews to exercise virtue, righteousness toward one another and piety toward God, and to come to baptism — and says many thought the destruction of Herod's army was divine punishment for killing him.

facts.title: Josephus explains why Herod feared John
facts.text: His account is political rather than personal: crowds were moved by John's preaching, Herod feared the influence might raise a rebellion, and thought it safer to strike first than to wait for trouble.

facts.title: There is a paragraph about Jesus in the Antiquities
facts.text: The passage known as the Testimonium Flavianum describes Jesus as a wise man and a doer of wonderful works, condemned by Pilate at the suggestion of the principal men. Its wording has been debated for centuries, with most scholars holding that a genuine notice was expanded by later Christian copyists.

facts.title: Pilate appears in Josephus as a governor who kept provoking riots
facts.text: He records Pilate bringing military standards bearing the emperor's image into Jerusalem by night, and spending Temple money on an aqueduct — both of which set off mass protest.

facts.title: Josephus records the death of Herod Agrippa in terms close to Acts
facts.text: He describes the king appearing in a garment of silver at Caesarea, the crowd hailing him as a god, and his sudden collapse into a fatal illness — an account that runs parallel to Acts 12.

facts.title: Judas the Galilean, mentioned by Gamaliel, is in Josephus too
facts.text: Gamaliel cites him in Acts 5 as a failed rebel. Josephus names him repeatedly as the author of the seditious teaching that eventually brought the nation to destruction, and describes the census revolt he led.

facts.title: Josephus records the stoning of James, the brother of Jesus
facts.text: He writes that the high priest Ananus convened the sanhedrim while one Roman procurator was dead and his replacement still on the road, and had James delivered to be stoned — an act that the more equitable citizens of Jerusalem protested against.

facts.title: The Temple system Hebrews argues against was still running when it was written
facts.text: Josephus describes the priestly courses, the daily sacrifices and the high priesthood as functioning institutions of his own early life. Hebrews argues that they are obsolete — while the smoke was still going up.

facts.title: Josephus lived through the destruction Revelation was written after
facts.text: He was a commander in the revolt, then a captive, and finally an eyewitness attached to the Roman camp at the siege. Antiquities was published around AD 93, within a couple of years of the traditional date for Revelation.

facts.title: Josephus tells the Maccabean revolt from the same sources
facts.text: Books XII and XIII of the Antiquities cover the ground of 1 Maccabees closely, and often follow it almost sentence for sentence. Where the Bible falls silent after Malachi, Josephus and Maccabees together are the main narrative witnesses to what happened.

facts.title: The eight-day rededication became Hanukkah
facts.text: Josephus records the purification of the Temple after its desecration and the festival established to mark it, noting that the Jews kept the feast for eight days and calling it the feast of Lights.

facts.title: Josephus preserves the Roman and Spartan correspondence
facts.text: The treaties 1 Maccabees quotes between the Jews and Rome, and the claim of kinship with the Lacedemonians, both reappear in Josephus, who collected such public decrees as documentary proof of Jewish standing abroad.

facts.title: Antiochus IV forbade the practice of the religion outright
facts.text: Josephus describes the king compelling Jews to sacrifice against their law and killing those who refused, which is the same persecution 2 Maccabees narrates from the martyrs' point of view.

facts.title: The murdered high priest Onias has a sequel in Josephus
facts.text: Josephus follows the family of Onias past his assassination to the temple his son later built at Leontopolis in Egypt — a second Jewish sanctuary outside Jerusalem that operated for more than two centuries.

facts.title: The high priest praised in Ecclesiasticus 50 is a historical figure
facts.text: Simon son of Onias, whom Ben Sira describes coming out from behind the veil, appears in Josephus among the high priests of the Second Temple — the book is praising a man its first readers could remember.

facts.title: Alexandria's Jewish community produced this kind of book
facts.text: Josephus describes the standing of Jews in Ptolemaic Egypt, including the translation of the law into Greek for the royal library. Wisdom of Solomon comes out of exactly that world: Jewish faith argued in Greek philosophical terms.

facts.title: Josephus retells the contest of the three guardsmen
facts.text: The scene where Zerubbabel wins Darius's favour by arguing that truth is stronger than wine, kings or women is not in Ezra — but Josephus includes it, apparently drawing on 1 Esdras or a shared source.

facts.title: Josephus confirms the Assyrian deportation Tobit lives through
facts.text: Tobit is set among the northern tribes carried to Nineveh and Media. Josephus records the same transplanting of the ten tribes by Shalmaneser, and the resettlement of foreigners in their place.

facts.title: Manasseh's captivity and repentance are in the record
facts.text: The prayer supplies what 2 Chronicles only refers to. Josephus likewise reports Manasseh taken by the Assyrians, brought low, and afterwards restored and reforming what he had corrupted.

facts.title: Baruch was a real scribe with a documented job
facts.text: Baruch son of Neriah wrote Jeremiah's scroll at his dictation and rewrote it after King Jehoiakim burned it. Josephus notes his learning and his closeness to the prophet through the fall of the city.

facts.title: Cyrus, who opens Bel and the Dragon, is Josephus's turning point
facts.text: Book XI of the Antiquities begins with Cyrus freeing the Jews. Bel and the Dragon places Daniel in the same court, which is why the story is attached to Daniel rather than told on its own.

facts.title: 2 Esdras asks the question Josephus lived through
facts.text: Its core was written after the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, asking why God allowed Rome to prosper. Josephus was present at that siege and wrote his own answer — a very different one, laying the blame on Jewish faction.

facts.title: The history in Judith is deliberately impossible
facts.text: The book calls Nebuchadnezzar king of the Assyrians reigning at Nineveh, though Josephus and the Bible both place him as king of Babylon after Nineveh had fallen. The mismatch is old, and is one reason the book has long been read as a parable.
